source_refs.quote: The appellant took on lease, the first floor of the premises in question from the respondent on January 22, 1964
for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

law_refs.quote: the premises let for residential purposes

tests.objects: Appellant as tenant; respondent as landlord; first-floor demised premises, distinct from landlord-occupied ground floor.
tests.opposition: The later proposed residential occupation of the first floor does not establish the purpose for which it was originally let.

opposition_refs.quote: that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

tests.gap_reason: The supplied lease record does not specify whether the first floor was let for residential purposes; intended later use does not decide the original letting purpose.
tests.rationale: A lease of the first floor is recorded, but the residential purpose of the letting, the literal predicate of C01, is not established. The owner's separate occupation of the ground floor cannot supply the missing term.

source_refs.quote: He also accepted his plea that the requirement of the landlord for his occupation was not bona fide.
It is the view of both the Tribunals that when eviction is asked for within about I I months of the letting, the claim of the landlord cannot be considered to be bonafide.

law_refs.quote: are required bona fide by the landlord for occupation as a residence

tests.objects: Respondent-landlord; first-floor demised premises; professed residential need for self and family.
tests.opposition: The landlord asserted genuine residential need, and a subsequent reported commissioner finding judged his occupied accommodation insufficient and unsuitable. That bears on adequacy of existing space but does not erase the prior adverse bona-fides findings.

opposition_refs.quote: that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.
the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient for a family consisting of the landlord, his wife, his son, son's wife and their children.
the premises in the occupation of the respondent were not reasonably suitable for his residence.

tests.rationale: The Controller accepted the tenant's objection and both Tribunals regarded the early filing as incompatible with bona fides. C02 is refuted at those stated prior levels; the later inadequacy assessment is substantial opposing material, not an automatic target-stage reversal.

source_refs.quote: that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

law_refs.quote: for himself or for any member of his family dependent on him

tests.objects: Respondent-landlord as intended occupant of the first floor; wife, son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren are additionally identified as family in a later report.
tests.opposition: The tenant disputed the genuineness of the need, but did not supply a competing identity for the proposed occupant; the dependency of any family member is not separately established.

opposition_refs.quote: He also contended that the landlord's requirement for his occupation was not bonafide.

tests.rationale: The landlord expressly sought residence for himself, satisfying the asserted self-occupation route regardless of whether family dependency is proved. This supports C03 at the stated-claim level without determining bona fides under C02.

source_refs.quote: The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises was then occupying the ground floor.

law_refs.quote: if he is the owner thereof

tests.objects: Respondent landlord; the whole property, including the demised first floor.
tests.opposition: No contrary assertion or ownership challenge appears in the allowed materials.
tests.rationale: The record expressly identifies the respondent landlord as owner of the entire property. The first floor belongs to the described entire premises, and ownership is distinct from the separate assessment of bona fide need.

source_refs.quote: for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

law_refs.quote: or for any person for whose benefit the premises are held

tests.objects: Respondent-owner and first floor; no separate person for whose benefit the premises were held is identified.
tests.opposition: The only stated occupation route is landlord self/family; the sources do not affirmatively negate every possible beneficiary arrangement.

opposition_refs.quote: for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members.

tests.rationale: There is no identified beneficiary-route transaction to evaluate. Because the self-occupation branch is expressly asserted, inventing a beneficiary or inferring absence of one from silence would misrate this independent alternative.

source_refs.quote: The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises was then occupying the ground floor.
the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient for a family consisting of the landlord, his wife, his son, son's wife and their children.
the premises in the occupation of the respondent were not reasonably suitable for his residence.

law_refs.quote: and that the landlord or such person has no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation.

tests.objects: Respondent landlord; first floor sought for eviction; ground floor occupied by landlord and assessed as unsuitable by a commissioner.
tests.opposition: The tenant disputed the landlord's bona fide need, while the commissioner later found the existing ground-floor accommodation unsuitable. The tenant's separate assertion about sufficiency of the tenant-occupied first floor is not a finding about an alternative residence for the landlord.

opposition_refs.quote: He also contended that the landlord's requirement for his occupation was not bonafide.

tests.gap_reason: The later finding addresses the landlord-occupied ground floor, but the supplied record does not establish whether the landlord had any additional reasonably suitable residence.
tests.rationale: The commissioner's unsuitability finding is material support concerning the known ground floor. It does not by itself prove the literal absence of every other reasonably suitable accommodation. The relevant absence proposition remains unresolved.

source_refs.quote: On or about September 10, 1959 the respondent landlord let out the premises in suit to the appellant
On 1-9- 1962 the respondent applied under

law_refs.quote: on or after the 9th day of June, 1952

tests.objects: Respondent landlord; appellant tenant; asserted subletting of shop to Sohan Singh during tenancy commencing in 1959.
tests.opposition: The appellant denied that any subletting occurred. No exact subletting date is given; the post-1952 conclusion concerns only the temporal setting of an alleged act by this tenant.

opposition_refs.quote: denied sub- letting.

tests.rationale: Any subletting by the appellant of a tenancy first created in September 1959 would necessarily postdate 9 June 1952, and the claim was filed in September 1962. This supports the date condition of the alleged disposition, not that any disposition occurred.

source_refs.quote: The Rent Controller was of the view that the appellant was the legally Wedded wife of Sohan Singh.
Sohan Singh and the appellant were living together as husband and wife and, therefore, there was no question of any sub--letting by the appellant of the premises.
That finding was confirmed in appeal by the Rent Control Tribunal, Delhi.
Neither any talks regarding sub-letting took place in my presence, nor the rent was paid in my presence,

law_refs.quote: In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant

tests.objects: Appellant tenant; Sohan Singh alleged subtenant and husband; Royal Dispensing Chemists and Druggists; entire shop.
tests.opposition: The landlord alleged a subtenancy and an exceptionally large rent paid by Sohan Singh. A typed document also recorded recognition of the appellant as his wife, and no direct witnessed rent payment was identified in the supplied testimony.

opposition_refs.quote: she had sub-let the entire premises to one Sohan Singh
It was further alleged that the appellant was charging a fabulous amount as rent from her sub-tenant Sohan Singh.
The true copy disclosed that the appellant was accepted as the wife of Sohan Singh.

tests.rationale: The Rent Controller's no-subletting conclusion, affirmed on appeal, refutes the asserted tenancy relationship at those prior stages. The contrary landlord allegations do not independently show rent paid, transfer of estate interest and a right to possession against the tenant.

source_refs.quote: she had sub-let the entire premises to one Sohan Singh
from the time of the lease the business of a Chemist was being run there in the premises by her husband and she also occasionally helped him in the running of the business.

law_refs.quote: In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.

tests.objects: Appellant tenant; Sohan Singh; shop; no separately described assignment.
tests.opposition: The pleaded theory was subletting to the husband, not a distinct assignment; his running a shop does not itself prove or disprove a transfer of all tenancy rights.

opposition_refs.quote: denied sub- letting.

tests.rationale: Nothing in the allowed record identifies an assignment arrangement to which the all-rights-divestment test can reliably be applied. The refusal to rate this unused alternative is not a finding of no assignment.

source_refs.quote: was running a business under the name of Royal Dispensing Chemists and Druggists in the shop.
from the time of the lease the business of a Chemist was being run there in the premises by her husband and she also occasionally helped him in the running of the business.

law_refs.quote: "parting with possession" must have been by the tenant.

tests.objects: Appellant tenant; Sohan Singh as person operating chemist shop; physical shop use versus legal right to possess it.
tests.opposition: The landlord alleged Sohan Singh was a subtenant. The appellant characterized him as her husband and herself as an occasional participant; the prior finding rejected subletting but did not expressly adjudicate a separate divestment of legal possession.

opposition_refs.quote: she had sub-let the entire premises to one Sohan Singh
Sohan Singh and the appellant were living together as husband and wife and, therefore, there was no question of any sub--letting by the appellant of the premises.

tests.gap_reason: No document or prior finding settles whether the appellant divested both physical possession and the legal right to possess the shop in favour of Sohan Singh. Operation of his business does not alone resolve those rights.
tests.rationale: Sohan Singh's business use could coexist with the appellant's tenancy rights. The prior no-subletting finding bears against exclusive transfer, yet does not resolve the distinct parting-with-possession requirements; C04 remains unresolved.

source_refs.quote: she had sub-let the entire premises to one Sohan Singh
denied sub- letting.

law_refs.quote: without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

tests.objects: Respondent landlord; appellant tenant; alleged disposition of whole shop to Sohan Singh.
tests.opposition: The landlord's allegation and the appellant's denial concern whether a disposition took place, not whether written consent had been given for it.

opposition_refs.quote: denied sub- letting.

tests.gap_reason: There is no stated written-consent instrument, denial of consent, or finding addressing whether consent in writing was obtained for the alleged Sohan Singh arrangement.
tests.rationale: Silence about written permission cannot support the required proposition that written consent was not obtained, irrespective of the prior rejection of subletting.

source_refs.quote: from the time of the lease the business of a Chemist was being run there in the premises by her husband and she also occasionally helped him in the running of the business.
Sohan Singh and the appellant were living together as husband and wife and, therefore, there was no question of any sub--letting by the appellant of the premises.
The true copy disclosed that the appellant was accepted as the wife of Sohan Singh.

law_refs.quote: If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession

tests.objects: Appellant tenant and alleged husband Sohan Singh; shop and claimed shared family/business use.
tests.opposition: The landlord alleged a separate shop subtenancy and substantial rent. A common marital household and occasional help are material to concurrent use, but do not themselves establish retained legal possession of this shop.

opposition_refs.quote: It was further alleged that the appellant was charging a fabulous amount as rent from her sub-tenant Sohan Singh.

tests.gap_reason: The record does not state whether the appellant continued to hold an enforceable right to concurrent use and legal possession of the shop, or whether an agreement wholly ousted her; business participation alone is not conclusive.
tests.rationale: Prior findings and the appellant's account support a retained-user explanation and weigh against total exclusion. But C06 asks specifically about legal possession of the relevant shop, for which the required right or ouster fact is not expressly resolved.

source_refs.quote: The premises consisted of a shop.
she had sub-let the entire premises to one Sohan Singh

law_refs.quote: the whole or any part of the premises

tests.objects: Entire shop demised to appellant; entire shop was the object of respondent's asserted transfer to Sohan Singh.
tests.opposition: The appellant denied subletting itself, not the identification of the shop as the premises alleged to have been transferred.

opposition_refs.quote: denied sub- letting.

tests.rationale: The alleged transaction expressly covers the whole demised shop, a statutorily included scope. C07 does not establish that a transfer actually took place.

tests.opposition: The statutory authorities referred to incidental commercial use; the High Court found the evidentiary basis for that use lacking. Neither proposition converts the expressly residential purpose of the original letting into a commercial letting.

This High Court found that there was no evidence for the statutory authorities to come to the conclusion, which they did, as regards the premises having been used for commercial purpose.

law_refs.quote: are required bona fide by the landlord for occupation as a residence

tests.objects: Respondent successor landlord; demised residential premises; intended personal/family residential use not identified in the allowed material.
tests.opposition: The lower authorities rejected applicability of the invoked clause based on commercial use, and the High Court questioned that evidentiary premise. Neither finding makes a direct positive or negative determination about the landlord's bona fide housing need.

opposition_refs.quote: had also been used incidentally for commercial purposes
there was no evidence for the statutory authorities to come to the conclusion

tests.gap_reason: No asserted residential need, intended use circumstances, or prior finding about bona fide requirement appears in the supplied materials; the records concern letting purpose, commercial use and paying guests.

so as to exclude the application of

law_refs.quote: for himself or for any member of his family dependent on him

tests.objects: Respondent successor landlord (daughter of original lessor); demised premises; no stated proposed residential occupant.
tests.opposition: The purchase identifies the landlord but supplies no statement about whether she herself, or a dependent family member, was intended to live in the premises.
tests.gap_reason: The record does not identify the person for whom residential occupation was being sought; it therefore cannot determine the self/dependent-family route.
tests.rationale: A person becoming landlord by purchase is not thereby shown to seek residential occupation herself or for a dependent family member. The proposed occupant's identity and route are decisive, not supplied.

source_refs.quote: The present respondent purchased the property from her father on 27th June, 1964 and thus stepped into his shoes as the `landlord' as defined under

law_refs.quote: if he is the owner thereof

tests.objects: Respondent daughter and purchaser/successor landlord; property comprising demised premises.
tests.opposition: No conflicting claim as to the respondent's purchase or ownership is included.
tests.rationale: The record expressly reports the respondent purchased the property from its previous owner. That supports ownership of the demised premises, independently of whether her residential occupation route is shown.

source_refs.quote: The respondent is the daughter of the original landlord
The present respondent purchased the property from her father on 27th June, 1964

law_refs.quote: or for any person for whose benefit the premises are held

tests.objects: Respondent successor owner; no identified third-party person for whose benefit the premises are held.
tests.opposition: The sale identifies the purchaser but states no arrangement of holding the property for another beneficiary. This omission does not disprove every possible beneficiary route.
tests.rationale: The independent beneficiary branch was not invoked by an identified person or holding arrangement. It is unrateable rather than refuted by the mere absence of an allegation.

source_refs.quote: The present respondent purchased the property from her father on 27th June, 1964
the premises which had been let out for residential purposes to the appellant

law_refs.quote: and that the landlord or such person has no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation.

tests.objects: Respondent successor owner; demised residential premises; no other dwelling of respondent or any beneficiary described.
tests.opposition: The parties' supplied dispute about student paying guests and commercial use speaks to use of the demised premises, not the landlord's other residential accommodation.

opposition_refs.quote: the foreign students who were lodging were her paying guests and were not her tenants.

tests.gap_reason: There is no information on whether the respondent, or any qualifying beneficiary, possessed or could use other reasonably suitable residential accommodation.
tests.rationale: Ownership of the rented premises and the tenant's paying-guest dispute do not establish the absence or suitability of other accommodation for the relevant claimant. C06 is factually unresolved.
